summary: Auxiliary products such as flight protection and flexible-change services are recommended alongside primary travel purchases. This setting creates a granularity ambiguity: SKUs within one product type share semantics but differ in price and coverage, while rejecting one offer does not imply disinterest in the entire type. We present \textbf{PEETS} (\textbf{P}reference-aware \textbf{E}mbeddings with \textbf{E}xplicit \textbf{T}ree \textbf{S}tructure), a training-time framework for auxiliary product bundling. PEETS regularizes an existing click--conversion predictor through two conditional comparisons. Hierarchical Contrastive Loss uses the pair's common ancestor as a reference; Negative Contrastive Loss conditions structural sampling and comparison shifts on logged rejection events. Both act on shared SKU representations during training. This separates catalog relatedness from individual preference supervision and leaves the predictive serving path intact. PEETS achieves 78.20\% AUC, exceeding TWIN V2 by 0.90 percentage points and the matched base model by 1.15 points. In a 14-day online evaluation, gross auxiliary GMV per exposed user-day improves by 8.20\% over Policies, 3.06\% over Base, and 0.84\% over TWIN V2, with all three user-bootstrap 95\% intervals above zero. Bundling rate is 0.51 points below Policies. The cancellation interval's upper limit exceeds the prespecified margin. PEETS adds no auxiliary-loss computation to serving and records 42.1~ms p95 latency, compared with 42.0~ms for Base.

title: Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity
summary:
We introduce NeSySy, a synthetic generator for neurosymbolic learning tasks that jointly produces logical constraints and consistent datasets. Unlike existing benchmarks, NeSySy provides fine-grained control over key properties such as constraint structure, tightness, input dependence, and data generation and alignment strategies. In particular, it allows the use of rich constraints over infinite domains, and uses solvers to ensure that the constraints are meaningful and that generated samples satisfy the constraints.
  We design NeSySy to support both learning with declarative constraints and learning from distant supervision. Across a range of constraint families, we provide evidence that its parameters induce systematic and largely independent effects on task difficulty. Using NeSySy, we study constraint-aware learning methods, identifying regimes where explicit constraint enforcement is beneficial and where expressive unconstrained models can instead learn constraint structure directly from data. Our results establish NeSySy as a controlled testbed for analysing the interaction between learning and logical structure.
  NeSySy is built around a pipeline that incorporates solvers. Satisfiability checkers (CNFgen and Z3) generate and certify constraints. Constrained optimizers (RC2 for MaxSAT, Z3 for OMT) compute optimal repairs that guarantee every generated sample is consistent.

title: Routing Beyond Task Categories: A Cost-Aware LAB-Bench Study
comment: 21 pages, 3 figures. Reproduction archive at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24220501
summary: We tested whether features of biology questions or of a model's first answer can improve accuracy within an inference budget. In a LAB-Bench pilot, we compared a category router with one that adds six structural features. Neither reached the primary 80% accuracy target on development. At the 50% and 60% secondary targets, both chose Haiku for all 120 held-out questions and scored 71/120. We then froze a new comparison before collecting responses on 144 additional questions. Semantic routing scored 86/144. A policy that could defer after reading Haiku's answer scored 87/144. Both stayed within the inference budget of USD 0.678 per 1,000 queries. Against a 95% Haiku and 5% GPT mixture, the accuracy gains were 0.66 percentage points for semantic routing and 1.35 points for deferral. The paired 95% intervals were [-0.28,2.25] and [-0.14,3.47] points. A simple rule that escalated Haiku nonanswers scored 92/144 at USD 0.710 per 1,000 queries, above the budget. A retrospective nonanswer rule with a calibration-selected escalation probability gave an expected 85.63/144. At the learned deferral policy's observed inference cost, post hoc interpolation gave an expected 86.14/144. In a later development check, Astra and Gemini each scored 30/40. The best tested policy in each router family matched that score. The pair covered 33/40 in hindsight. The routers missed the 32/40 criterion, so the proposed 120-question evaluation did not start.

title: Before the Word: Name Information in Description-Derived States of Small Language Models, With and Without Naming Failure
comment: 22 pages, 9 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24228887
summary: The tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state, knowing an object but not its name, motivates this study as an analogy only. We ask whether small language models form a name-predictive state from a name-free description, and whether it differs when naming fails but description selection succeeds. In an internally pre-registered study (a frozen document, no external registry) of Qwen2-0.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and Phi-3-mini with 200 items, we combine a similarity read-out, a Patchscopes-style read-out and activation patching with matched controls. H1 (name information in the state) was supported in all nine model-by-description-type combinations; the agreement rule was met by the similarity measure together with patching, while Patchscopes stayed near chance. Post-hoc robustness checks after internal review (logit lens, single-position patch, manipulation check) temper this reading: name information in middle layers is clearest under the multi-position patch and the similarity measure, and weak under single-position patching at 50% depth. H2' (description-paraphrase consistency of name-free states not lower in failure items) is mixed: the SmolLM2 deficit test is significant under the pre-registered specification but not robust; Phi-3 non-inferiority holds across margins and a word-overlap covariate, although its bootstrap interval includes zero; Qwen2-0.5B is inconclusive. A capacity explanation remains untested. We report vehicle-level signals only, not meaning.

title: GainCtrl: Predicting Remaining Gains for Efficient LLM Agent Execution
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to power agents that interact with tools and environments to solve complex tasks. Repeated attempts improve the quality of tool-using agents, but continued execution incurs additional costs even when it is unlikely to improve the best result ultimately returned. This raises the question of when to stop an attempt to reduce execution cost while preserving task-level Best-of-N quality. To address this question, we introduce GainCtrl, a gain-based execution controller for LLMs. In GainCtrl, a lightweight CPU predictor uses interaction histories to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores, which are then used to guide stopping decisions with calibrated thresholds to limit the loss in mean Best-of-N task quality. We evaluate the controller through trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors. Comparisons of interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers show that GainCtrl generally uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality. Fixed policies also achieve quality close to that of full execution while substantially reducing token consumption. The predictor runs at millisecond latency on a single CPU thread, supporting repeated monitoring without access to LLM internals.

title: Well-Log Reconstruction with Pre-trained Geological Knowledge: A Knowledge-Conditioned Large-Language-Model Generative Agent
summary: Missing well-log intervals make subsurface reconstruction ill-posed. Existing numerical regression models lack geological prior knowledge to constrain ambiguous inverse mappings. We propose GeoLog-Agent, a knowledge-conditioned generative agent using pre-trained large language models (LLMs) as a source of geological priors. A universal Geo-Harness translates LLM stratigraphic reasoning into formation-anchored petrophysical trajectories, feature-wise linear modulation, and conditional adversarial constraints. On the Norwegian North Sea benchmark, GeoLog-Agent achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.9307 and a peak $R^2$ of 0.9713. It exceeds the nine-baseline average $R^2$ of 0.8387 by 0.0920, with a 30.97% average RMSE reduction, and exceeds the strongest baseline by 0.0274--0.0498 in $R^2$, with 16.25%--24.05% lower RMSE. Ablations confirm the effectiveness and synergy of geological prior reasoning, multi-scale dilated generation, and conditional adversarial modules. Transferring the coupling mechanism to six conventional deep learning models improves their $R^2$ by 0.0162--0.0789 with cross-well stability. These results demonstrate how foundation-model domain reasoning can constrain deep generative reconstruction of missing petrophysical measurements.

title: EEGProbe: Do Vision-Language Models Really Understand EEG? A Benchmark for Signal-Grounded EEG Signals Evaluation
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification. We evaluate 11 representative open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The strongest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves an overall score of only 41.63\%, with cross-modal EEG alignment emerging as a major bottleneck. We further examine model behavior from a neurophysiological perspective and analyze how temporal, spectral, spatial, and physiological EEG structure relates to model successes and failures. Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can reshape model predictions by helping models recognize the neurophysiological patterns present in the input and connect them with relevant neurological knowledge, narrowing the gap between general multimodal competence and EEG understanding. EEGProbe provides a testbed for current VLMs and a basis for developing future multimodal models that can interpret EEG evidence more reliably. The EEGProbe benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/2122ZHU/EEGProbe.

title: Robust Well-Log Reconstruction Across Point Gaps and Whole Wells via Boundary-Gated Soft-Thresholding Kalman Fusion
summary: Missing wireline logs hinder subsurface characterization. Deep reconstruction networks suffer from gap-boundary steps and cross-basin shifts, while interpolation and Gaussian smoothers struggle with long intervals and outliers. We propose boundary-gated soft-thresholding Kalman fusion (ST-KF), unifying multiresolution wavelet shrinkage, distance-gated residual prior learning, and closed-form robust Kalman smoothing with learning--inference decoupling. Across two public benchmarks totaling 263 wells in the Norwegian North Sea and New Zealand's Taranaki Basin, ST-KF ranks first over 0.15--100-m anchored gaps with 0.09% parameter overhead. Against the strongest of nine baselines, pooled RMSE falls by 5.0%--8.3% for bulk density and 6.4%--15.6% for compressional slowness; against the four strongest baselines, reductions are 0.7%--4.1% for neutron porosity and 1.3%--2.9% for photoelectric factor. Ablations and sensitivity analyses confirm operator synergy and stable performance: removing state-space fusion increases short-gap errors by up to 58.8%, while zero-shot transfer cuts anchored errors by 14%--68%. The results show that local borehole continuity transfers across basins whereas cross-property mappings shift with regional geology, supporting measurement-guided log reconstruction.

title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
summary: Uplift modeling estimates the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and supports industrial decisions such as promotional pricing. When large language models (LLMs) encode product text, treatment-revealing content can introduce shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose \emph{LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization} (\textsc{LULR}), which uses a CLUB-based penalty on the causal head's trainable shared representation while keeping the LLM encoder frozen. Controlled proxy experiments show a positive ranking-score interaction and higher scores than the tested weight-decay configuration; treatment-dependent evaluation limits their interpretation to exploratory model behavior. Structured-only comparisons provide reference performance, without establishing a general advantage over tree-based estimators. On a million-record industrial pricing RCT, \textsc{LULR} improves offline $\text{lift@}0.3$ in $4/5$ seeds, although the difference is not statistically significant and estimated policy values are near-tied. A separate one-week online A/B experiment records $5.45\%$ higher sales volume and $1.91\%$ higher GMV than the control arm. These aggregate results provide short-term business evidence for the complete deployed pricing policy; they do not isolate the regularizer's contribution.

title: Multi-Objective Causal Bandits: Minimal Intervention Space and Policy-Level Learning
comment: To appear in Proceedings of NeurIPS 26
summary: Many decision-making problems involve multiple objectives, where actions affect several performance metrics, fairness criteria, or safety constraints. We study multi-objective causal bandits with multiple reward nodes, where actions correspond to interventions on subsets of variables in a causal graph and performance is evaluated through Pareto optimality. Existing approaches to multi-objective bandits often rely on pairwise Pareto dominance or optimize a fixed scalarization. However, pairwise comparisons alone can fail to identify actions dominated by randomized policies, whose expected reward vectors lie in the convex hull of action-level rewards. Thus, an intervention may be suboptimal even if no single intervention dominates it, because it can be dominated by a randomized policy over other interventions. We formalize this policy-level phenomenon and show that it has consequences for both causal action-space reduction and online learning. First, we provide a necessary-and-sufficient graphical characterization of possibly Pareto- optimal minimal intervention sets. Our characterization yields a minimal, sound, and complete candidate intervention family from the graph alone, correcting prior formulations that may include intervention sets that are never Pareto-optimal under any compatible structural causal model. Second, over this reduced intervention space, we design an online UCB-style algorithm that eliminates actions using dominance tests against convex combinations of other actions, and prove logarithmic gap-dependent Pareto regret. Finally, we study constrained multi-objective causal bandits, where feasibility and optimality may be realized only with randomized policies, and develop an online UCB-style constrained bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and constraint-violation guarantees.

title: ForeSay: Tell the Future in Words, Branch the Details in Noise for Precipitation Nowcasting
summary: Precipitation nowcasting involves two distinct scales of uncertainty: macroscopic storm evolution and fine-scale local convective variations. Current generative ensemble methods entangle both scales within independent random noise draws. This coupling causes two practical limitations: every ensemble member must execute the full sampling trajectory from scratch, so an N-member ensemble costs N times a single forecast; moreover, divergent trajectories spatially misalign heavy-rain echoes across members, causing standard pixel-wise averaging to blur critical high-intensity extremes. We present ForeSay, a generative nowcasting framework that decouples macroscopic evolution prediction from local stochastic detail generation. Given historical radar frames, a vision-language model first predicts a textual scenario of future storm dynamics to condition a Rectified Flow generator. Guided by this shared macroscopic prior, ensemble members share early trunk sampling steps to establish the storm trajectory and branch with fresh noise only in later steps to explore local convective details. Because members then differ mainly in local details, self-anchored support-consensus decoding replaces pixel averaging with discrete support voting to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores. Across six datasets, ForeSay achieves the best CSI at the highest precipitation thresholds, with relative improvements over the strongest baseline on each dataset ranging from over 10% to 84%. Our 8-member ensemble retains the forecasting skill and diversity of eight independently sampled runs while reducing computational cost from 8x to 5.2x that of a single forecast.

title: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
summary: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. During autoregressive decoding, however, generating each token requires several sequential passes through these layers, leading to high decoding latency. Pipelined self-speculative methods use shallow-loop predictions to process tokens at different loops in the same batch, but each token must reach the drafting depth before the next can enter the pipeline. We introduce LoopFill, a training-free speculative decoding algorithm for looped LLM that combines multi-token suffix drafts with shallow-loop predictions in a single draft tree. Both drafters contribute to one tree, so a suffix lookup can immediately extend a shallow prediction and several future tokens can enter the pipeline together. The shared block computes the highest-scoring draft candidates at different loop depths in one batch, and full-depth verification preserves the model's autoregressive output distribution. Across seven benchmarks, LoopFill's average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding is $5.85\times$ on Ouro-2.6B and $5.13\times$ on Huginn-3.5B. The speedups exceed those of LoopAhead, the strongest baseline, by \(40\%\) on Ouro-2.6B and \(25\%\) on Huginn-3.5B.

title: Conversing with a Conversational Agent: A Real Conversation, Not a Simulated One
summary: The claim that interactions with artificial conversational agents merely simulate human conversation rests on a philosophical distinction between reproducing the observable features of an activity and actually performing it. Although this distinction is appropriate for certain physical phenomena, its application to linguistic and symbolic activities is far less straightforward. This article argues that conversations with large language model (LLM)-based agents are genuine conversational activities rather than mere simulations, without thereby attributing consciousness, subjective understanding, or human intentionality to artificial systems. Drawing on the distinction between subjective and objective simulation, the article first examines the limitations of defining conversation exclusively through the intrinsic properties of its participants. It then develops a relational and semiotic account of conversational activity, informed by linguistic pragmatics, Lacan's Conversing with a Conversational Agent theory of the mirror, Baudrillard's concept of the simulacrum, Simondon's philosophy of individuation, and Peirce's semiotics. These perspectives make it possible to distinguish the reality of conversational interaction from the appearance of artificial subjectivity and from the epistemic validity of the meanings produced. The argument culminates in the concept of Hybrid Semiotic Fabrication, which characterizes meaning-making as a distributed process involving human participants, artificial intelligence, corpora, and technical arrangements. Recognizing the reality of human-AI conversation therefore entails neither anthropomorphizing artificial agents nor granting their outputs epistemic authority. Rather, it requires a more precise account of the relational, semiotic, and normative conditions under which conversational meaning is produced and justified.

title: With the Right Representation, Classical Machine Learning Rivals Deep Models for Olfactory Mixture Similarity
summary: Modeling olfactory mixtures remains a critical challenge in machine olfaction because the task requires reasoning over relationships between sets of odorants rather than over individual molecules in isolation. However, prior comparisons between deep and classical approaches also varied how the relationship between the two mixtures was represented, since the classical baselines primarily relied on weak representations that described each mixture independently and provided little direct signal about how the mixtures differed. In this work, we revisit classical learning using explicit symmetric comparison features on unordered pairs of mixtures, evaluating these representations with XGBoost and kernel ridge regression (KRR). We find that XGBoost with explicit comparison features achieves performance competitive with specialized deep mixture models on the main benchmark. Ablation studies show that coordinate-wise absolute differences alone provide strong predictive performance, while combining them with sums and products yields further improvements. KRR also benefits substantially from explicit comparison features, with further gains from appropriate kernel choice and preprocessing. Overall, these results suggest that explicitly encoding how two mixtures differ is an important ingredient for classical machine learning in low-data olfactory mixture prediction.

title: DetourBench: Trajectory-Level Evaluation of Interactive Agents with Exact Minimum-Action Bounds
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Evaluation of Interactive Agents
summary:
Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists.
  We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count $L_0$ with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work $R_T$, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/DatagridsAI/DetourBench.

title: BadGCL: Towards Persistent Backdoor Attack on Graph Continual Learning Systems
summary: Backdoor attacks pose a persistent security threat to machine learning systems, yet their behavior under graph continual learning (GCL) remains underexplored. Conventional graph backdoor attacks often lose effectiveness as models are updated across successive tasks, creating the impression that continual updates naturally weaken malicious associations. This work reveals a contrasting vulnerability: knowledge-preservation mechanisms in GCL can also preserve early injected backdoors when the poisoned update is compatible with the clean-task signal being retained. For graph data, this risk is amplified by structural triggers, which are embedded into the message-passing paths of graph neural networks (GNNs) and can induce stable representation shifts across tasks. To expose this risk, we propose BadGCL, a model-agnostic framework for persistent backdoor attacks under a strict early-stage intervention setting. BadGCL learns topology-aware structural triggers using a gradient mutual-information objective that couples poisoned gradients with clean-task optimization signals, together with a propagation consistency objective that stabilizes trigger-induced effects through graph message passing. We provide theoretical analysis showing that gradient compatibility and propagation stability jointly support long-term backdoor persistence under benign continual updates. Extensive experiments across task-IL and class-IL protocols, four GCL benchmarks, and diverse victim systems show that BadGCL achieves persistent attack effectiveness with limited clean-utility degradation, substantially outperforming graph and continual-learning backdoor baselines and remaining robust against representative defenses.

title: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization
comment: 49 pages, 8 figures. Work by Bowen Liu was done during an internship at Tencent Hy Team. Yuhan Li is Project Lead; Nuo Chen is corresponding author (chennuo26@gmail.com). Project page: https://acceleratebench.com/
summary: Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.

title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
summary: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

title: From Recursion to Convolution: Parallel Self-Improvement for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent self-improvement enables agents to improve through interaction and feedback. However, sequential dependencies across agents and refinement rounds can propagate errors, increase computational costs, and limit parallelism. Moreover, refining individual features or agents in isolation can overlook their dependencies and restrict collective coordination. To address these challenges, we propose ConvRSI, a framework for parallelizing multi-agent self-improvement through convolution. ConvRSI couples intra-agent convolution, which jointly refines related agent features, with inter-agent graph convolution, which aggregates messages according to the collaboration topology. Both stages operate in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeatedly decoding and re-encoding intermediate messages. Experiments on MATH-500 show that ConvRSI achieves 5.04% performance improvement while reducing 17.27% inference cost, and 45.11% latency compared with RecursiveMAS. It also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing their topologies as adjacency matrices. These results demonstrate the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. Our code and datasets are provided in https://github.com/LYA2333/ConvRSI.

title: Score-Based Stochastic Closure Modeling via Offline Indirect Learning and Online Data Assimilation
summary: Stochastic closure modeling is an emerging area in reduced-order modeling of large and complex (e.g., multiscale, multi-physics) systems, for which the computationally affordable reduced-order physical descriptions (e.g., digital twins for additive manufacturing, world models for AI agents) in numerical simulations inevitably lead to information losses that cannot be well addressed by classical deterministic closures. However, learning stochastic closures typically requires closure data that are difficult to obtain from measurements or often prohibitively expensive to compute using first-principles simulations. In this work, we develop a stochastic closure modeling framework that builds on score-based diffusion models, leveraging indirect offline training and online data assimilation without requiring the direct data of closures. Numerical experiments on two-dimensional turbulent flows demonstrate that indirect offline learning captures key closure statistics and improves predictions of system state. In addition, combining the learned closure with known physical dynamics leads to better generalization capability across different regimes than purely data-driven models that directly predict system state. Compared to standard data assimilation methods with a Gaussian assumption, the posterior-score assimilation better represents non-Gaussian features of the learned closure, and its combination with state-level data assimilation further improves prediction of the system state. The proposed framework enables stochastic closure modeling in realistic and challenging scenarios of complex dynamical systems in mechanics and engineering problems, where non-Gaussian statistics of model-form uncertainties are non-negligible (e.g., due to the nonlinearities of the system dynamics and/or the observations) and true closure data are not available, for both offline learning and online assimilation.

title: Which AI Use Cases Deserve a Pilot? A Risk and Value Framework for Funding, Scoping, and Scaling AI
comment: 18 pages. All results use synthetic data. A companion Python package reproduces the tables
summary: A composite score can rank AI use cases while leaving the permitted operating scope and the evidence required for expansion unspecified. We treat the unit of decision as a use case at a proposed scope (authority, human mediation, limits, volume, environment, population) and define three decisions: screen the scope, fund the experiment, and authorize expansion only when residual risk is acceptable and evidence of incremental net value applies at that scope. A risk track (R1-R4) is implemented as an explicit decision table with vetoes and documented precedence, and a value track follows four evidence stages with each transition needing its own evidence. Funding uses expected value of perfect information as an upper bound and the value of sample information for the specific experiment. A quantified expected-loss check, required where policy says so, computes the containment an expansion needs and credits a control only on evidence measured at the proposed scope; in a synthetic scenario the highest-value control design fails that test while a smaller scope passes. A reproducible Python package with 279 passing tests demonstrates the framework on synthetic refund, reconciliation and knowledge-assistant use cases, including a synthetic matched-scope fixture and a transferability stress test (value evidence is simulated, not realized), and compares it with a public AWS sample. Thresholds and appetite are prototype policy requiring field validation.

title: RIFT: Reward Improvement Field Transfer for Cross-Domain Offline RL
comment: 39 pages, 4 figures, 17 tables (10 pages main text; remainder references and appendices)
summary: Learning from limited target data is a central challenge in cross-domain offline reinforcement learning. Abundant source data can help, but dynamics differences can make direct transition reuse unreliable. We propose Reward Improvement Field Transfer (RIFT), which instead learns how low- and high-reward source transitions differ. RIFT encodes source and target transitions in a shared latent space, pairs low- and high-reward source transitions using optimal transport, and fits an affine field to their displacements. It applies this field to low-reward target anchors and decodes the results to augment the target dataset. The approach builds on the hypothesis that related domains can share useful low-to-high reward structure despite different dynamics. We bound synthesis error under shared class geometry, identify conditions favoring target anchoring over source-high transplant, and derive a conditional connection to downstream return. Experiments on dense-reward locomotion tasks under gravity, morphology, and friction shifts show improved aggregate performance over existing baselines.

title: Multi-LLM Agentic AI at the Edge: Joint Agent Scheduling and Resource Allocation
summary: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.

title: Elicited Adaptation: Auditable Localized Fairness via Pairwise Queries
summary: How much must a predictor's scores change when a community's elicited fairness standard changes? Similarity and tolerance judgments define protected comparisons and acceptable score gaps. We study minimum uniform score movement on a fixed pool of $n$ profiles. For scores satisfying a source standard, we characterize the exact cost of retaining that standard during adaptation: runs of consecutive target constraints along shortest paths determine the optimal amplification factor. Its sharp worst case is $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, and a full cost curve describes finite target-only repair budgets. Committing before the target is known can cost $n-1$ times the worst repair after revelation, even within one fixed convex ball of two-dimensional Mahalanobis metrics. Positive edge-budget floors cap both factors; bounded geometry also limits the commitment cost. At two interior targets of the construction attaining the $n-1$ bound, similarity queries alone yield a feasible $2$-approximate repair for tolerance $\eps\le1/[2(n-1)]$, reducing movement relative to common repair by a factor linear in $n$. Feasible $(1+α)$-optimal repair on this family has worst-case tolerance-query complexity $Θ(α^{-2}n^2\log(1/δ))$ under a fixed-slope logistic model. The analysis separates the information needed for a substantial adaptation benefit from the precision needed for nearly optimal movement. Elicitation studies and training comparisons examine tolerance choice and the relation between numerical compliance and predictive utility.

title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
comment: 33 pages, 19 tables, 8 figures; interactive web demos available at https://kkfyuen.github.io/cpcHCADDemos ; source code and datasets at https://github.com/kkfyuen/cpcHCADDemos ; archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23434993 ; earlier preprint version available at SSRN 4048692 (http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4048692 or https://ssrn.com/abstract=4048692)
summary: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

title: MathaMAGICal: Validating Trajectory Data Attribution During Capability Acquisition
summary: Influence-function-based methods like MAGIC provide exact first-order scores for trajectory data attribution, yet only retraining indicates whether those scores accurately predict data removal. We evaluate MAGIC on $86$M- and $152$M-parameter GPT-2-style models learning multistep arithmetic from scratch on filtered web text and four synthetic math families. Full-run attribution at $86$M suffers from numerical overflow, and even with metagradient clipping, scores correlate near chance with retraining (linear datamodeling score, LDS, $0.17$--$0.22$). In contrast, short checkpoint windows yield stable, accurate predictions at both scales (LDS $0.86$--$0.99$ across four $100$-step windows at $152$M), whereas a single-checkpoint gradient-dot baseline shows near-zero correlation. Rankings of individual training blocks predict retraining only within that single run and do not transfer across seeds or hyperparameters ($ρ\le 0.09$), whereas format-level patterns replicate across runs. Two data families, worked examples and primitive facts, occupy $2.1$--$2.6\times$ their corpus share in both the helpful and harmful $5\%$ score tails, reflecting strong bidirectional local sensitivity distinct from net benefit under multi-epoch family deletion. These results show that trajectory attribution is reliable within short, validated windows and yields family-level insights that generalize across runs.

title: Razavi-Bench: Tracking AI Progress in Analog Circuit Reasoning
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Project page: https://razavi-bench.tokenzhang.com ; code and data: https://github.com/Arcadia-1/razavi-bench
summary: We propose Razavi-Bench, a benchmark built from the 50 questions in Razavi's two Analog Design Experiments With AI articles and graded by GPT-6 Luna against reference answers and rubrics, and use it to track how fast AI models improve at analog circuit analysis. Across 73 multimodal large language models released between May 2024 and November 2026, the top score rose from 28.83% to 98.33% in 30 months, mostly before the reference answers were published. The leading models now answer almost every textbook question correctly; the hardest questions show a circuit that resembles a textbook one but works differently, or ask about behavior the obvious analysis misses. Within two and a half years, a set of questions that exposed the limits of AI models has become one they answer almost perfectly.

title: Data Attribution Should Steer Pretraining
comment: Accepted to the 3rd Workshop on Attributing Model Behavior at Scale: Data Attribution and Provenance (ATTRIB 2026) at NeurIPS 2026, Idea Track. 4 pages main text, 13 pages total, 1 figure, 2 tables
summary: Pretraining data curation decides what a model learns from, yet what makes a document worth learning from depends on what the model already knows. Influence-driven selectors already rank documents to improve one run; we argue that training-data attribution should steer pretraining by identifying testable data properties that become reusable curation criteria, evaluated on new data against cheaper selectors at matched total cost, discovery included. A document ranking is consumed by the run it was computed for, whereas an explained data property can be tested across corpora and checkpoints, especially where familiar quality signals diverge from measured usefulness. Because historical contribution, an understandable explanation, and future data value require distinct evidence, we specify a feedback loop that interprets attributed sources, tests candidate data changes, and states for five claim types what evidence each requires and what none establishes. We close with a falsifiable comparison against perplexity, classifier, and mixing baselines at equal total compute.

title: Jev-as-a-Reward: Validating Probabilistic Safety Judges for Reinforcement Learning
summary: Probabilistic safety judges return the probability of a safety label and cheaply score reinforcement learning rollouts. A confidence gate sends only uncertain verdicts to a stronger LLM judge, which leaves confidently passed harm in a blind spot. Policies can exploit this blind spot, and commercial judges release new versions. We propose a protocol that validates such a judge before and during training, separates the share of confidently passed harm from its amount, and re-validates it after each judge change. We apply it to two versions of Jev, a commercial decision-only judge, and to an open guard classifier. Under the probability reward of Jev, passed harm shrinks in all 11 runs under the primary reference, mostly more slowly than caught harm, and concentrates in the blind spot. Binarizing this judge meets the escape criterion on Llama, and the open guard classifier shows an escape signal in one seed under a second reference. Guard classifiers share this blind spot, and even frontier LLM judges catch at most one of 10 human-labeled confident misses. Without a trained reward model, the probability reward with a helpfulness term lowers HarmBench attack success on Llama-3.1-8B from 0.287 to at most 0.033 at the final checkpoint.

title: Where Should LLM Agents Adapt at Test Time? In Context, in Weights, or Both
summary: LLM agents operating repeatedly in the same environment, such as a code repository, a database, or an application suite, encounter tasks that share latent structure. Experience can reveal this structure, allowing agents to reuse environment knowledge and learn from environmental feedback. Agents can adapt at test-time using this experience through two channels: retaining it in context and updating their weights. These channels are usually studied separately, leaving unclear what each contributes and when they complement each other. We compare in-context learning (ICL), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using GRPO, and self-distillation using SDPO, alone and in combination, using a shared online protocol and modular framework. Agents encounter matched task streams, are evaluated on each task before adapting to it, and learn only from their own attempts and environment feedback. We evaluate 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline with Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments drawn from SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite, using five task orders per environment. ICL provides the largest standalone gain: its best policy raises mean success across environments from 28.8% to 49.4%. Adding GRPO to this policy achieves the highest mean success, 51.6%. While adding GRPO improves the overall mean under every ICL policy, SDPO has mixed effects. Trace analyses show fewer lookups and shorter attempts under ICL, consistent with reusing knowledge of the shared structure. However, ICL also frequently skips inspection and verification for the current task. Adding GRPO to ICL helps restore these behaviors while preserving its reduced environment lookups. These observations suggest that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can refine how agents use retained experience, motivating the joint study of context management and weight updates.

title: Hilbert States for Decision-Making under Partial Observability
summary: Decision-making under partial observability can be fundamentally limited by information, even with known dynamics: distinct physical states can induce the same observation history while favoring different actions. We study three questions: when is full-state optimality unattainable, what information exactly preserves the best observation-based decision, and how does finite-data learning affect reliability? First, we characterize decision ambiguity through conditional action preferences. We give a zero-regret criterion, a positive lower bound for conflicting uniquely optimal actions on positive-probability regions with uniformly positive cost gaps, and an exact binary-action regret formula. This also shows why physical-state ambiguity alone need not cause decision loss. Second, for two actions and squared terminal-goal costs in the plane, we derive an exact inner-product representation of conditional expected cost differences using three conditional moment contrasts and a goal-dependent feature. This Hilbert state preserves observation-optimal actions without hidden-state reconstruction. Under nondegenerate history and goal variation, its three-dimensional form is minimal among exact bilinear cost-contrast representations. Third, we relate finite-data state errors to excess decision regret via goal-projected errors, action margins, and goal geometry. Physics-based simulations verify information-limited regret, exact action preservation, and the role of second moments. Held-out real-SAR experiments demonstrate feasible goal-conditioned decisions from masked images, while finite-data evaluations reveal goal-dependent reliability. Together, these results separate irreducible information loss, exact representation sufficiency, and learning-induced excess regret.

title: Multiaccuracy as an Error Benchmark for Learning with Distribution Shift
summary:
Agnostic learning has a well-developed theory of computational and statistical complexity. For learning with distribution shift, even the choice of an appropriate error benchmark remains challenging. Testable learning with distribution shift (TDS) was introduced to develop computational foundations for this setting: using labeled training data and unlabeled test data, the learner must either produce a predictor with low test error or detect distribution shift. However, standard agnostic TDS guarantees allow a constant-factor amplification of the optimum error even when the training and test distributions coincide. They therefore do not directly recover the guarantee of classical agnostic learning.
  We introduce shift multiaccuracy, a stronger error benchmark inspired by multiaccuracy from algorithmic fairness. This yields a TDS formulation that becomes equivalent to multiaccuracy when there is no shift. Using a recent nontrivial reduction from agnostic learning to multiaccurate prediction from prior work, we obtain the first TDS framework that formally generalizes agnostic learning through an efficient reduction preserving the training marginal. The framework retains existing algorithmic upper bounds and inherits computational lower bounds from agnostic learning. Moreover, we establish a direct connection between our model and identity testing, yielding the first statistical characterization of agnostic TDS learning, in terms of Rademacher complexity.
  More broadly, we argue that shift multiaccuracy might be of independent interest in unsupervised domain adaptation, as it leads to sharper out-of-distribution generalization guarantees, and can be minimized directly, since its definition does not involve the unobserved test labels.

title: GRACE: Parallel Best-of-N Multi-Agent Analysis of Closed-Form Questions over Dataframes with Guardrail Selection and Adaptive Retry
comment: Accepted at the 5th Italian Conference on Big Data and Data Science (ITADATA 2026). To appear in CEUR Workshop Proceedings
summary: LLM agents answer closed-form questions over a tabular dataframe by writing and executing Python, almost always as a single rollout: one interpretation, one script, one result, accepted without comparison. The few pipelines that produce several candidates reconcile them by answer-agreement voting, which needs a single comparable scalar and always returns one, even when every candidate is wrong. We present GRACE (Generative, Ranked, Adaptive Code Ensemble), a production-oriented pipeline that instead runs parallel best-of-N selection specialised to dataframe code. N agents run concurrently under a strict, machine-checkable output contract, diversified by persona hints, per-retry rotation, and a two-regime temperature schedule. Rather than vote, GRACE judges the executed artefacts: a pairwise tournament pre-filters the pool and a domain-specialised guardrail either selects the best candidate or, when none is defensible, rejects the whole pool and abstains with a diagnosis (an option voting structurally lacks), which in turn drives an adaptive retry with per-agent feedback. On InfiAgent-DABench (DAEval, M = 246), using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the backbone, GRACE raises answer match from 39% for a single-rollout baseline to 71% (+32 pp, 1.8x), recovering 53% of previously wrong answers. On the same DAEval task, the smaller dense Qwen3.5-9B lifts answer match from 38% to 63% (+25 pp, 1.7x). A controlled 3 x 3 study that sweeps the number of parallel agents against the retry budget finds, on the 35B backbone, the two levers largely substitutable: once either one is generous, the other adds little, identifying a cheap operating point for deployment. The same directional pattern replicates on the independent DataBench benchmark, again on the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone, where answer match rises by 15 percentage points (from 70% to 85%) across 400 sampled questions.

title: Sample-Efficient Ensemble Reinforcement Learning at Scale
summary: Ensemble methods such as MeanQ have been shown to improve the sample efficiency of relatively small model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) architectures, including DQN and similarly sized variants such as Rainbow. However, to our knowledge, the effects of ensembling on large-scale architectures such as Bigger Better Faster (BBF) have not been studied. In this work, we present MeanQ-BBF, a hybrid model-free algorithm that combines the principles of MeanQ and BBF. Through statistically rigorous evaluation on the Atari 100K benchmark, we show that in contrast to naive scaling of the network size of BBF, which degrades performance, MeanQ-BBF is able to leverage the increase in model capacity to improve performance over BBF. Moreover, MeanQ-BBF does this in a computationally efficient way by organizing the added parameters into largely independent learners. Finally, we discuss the performance-cost tradeoff in the context of practical sample-efficient RL.

title: Hivemind: A Federated Protocol for AI-Mediated Tacit Knowledge Sharing in Organisations
summary: This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction. Individual AI memory systems capture the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during AI-assisted work. Hivemind creates the shared space in which this captured knowledge can flow between individuals across team and departmental boundaries, addressing a structural gap that neither centralised knowledge repositories nor existing AI tooling closes, even where partial solutions such as expert-finding systems exist. The paper evaluates centralised versus decentralised design approaches, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's (1995) Socialisation, Externalisation, Combination and Internalisation (SECI) model, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept implementation using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology. Measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains an open task for future work.

title: Exploration of Reinforcement Learning in Generative Recommendation Models
summary:
Traditional cascaded recommender systems balance accuracy and efficiency over large item spaces, but misaligned stage-wise objectives hinder end-to-end optimization. Generative recommendation unifies these stages in an autoregressive framework, providing a natural interface for reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize the entire generation process. However, directly applying RL often leads to unstable optimization and degraded recommendation quality.
  We revisit Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and other ratio-based objectives through a unified logit-gradient view. We identify three issues: (i) clipped surrogates create dead-gradient regions, under-utilizing samples; (ii) negative-advantage updates can become effectively unbounded as importance ratios grow, allowing a small subset of negatives to dominate optimization; and (iii) ratio-based control lacks sensitivity to absolute policy confidence, so updates on high-confidence cases may fail to vanish.
  Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose \emph{Gradient-Bounded Policy Optimization} (GBPO), a simple objective with stop-gradient normalization that is simultaneously (a) fully gradient-active, (b) sign-symmetrically bounded for both positive and negative updates, and (c) explicitly confidence-weighted under current policy probabilities. This ensures that updates gracefully vanish for $π\!\to\!1$ positives and $π\!\to\!0$ negatives. Across the evaluated settings, GBPO achieves competitive recommendation performance with more stable training than competing RL methods.

title: K2-Horizon: A Frontier Fleet of Open Source Language Models
summary: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/

title: When Does an AUROC Comparison Survive a Change in Population Mix?
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Does an AUROC comparison survive a change in the proportions of tasks, populations, or image corruptions? A pooled-AUROC ranking of failure detectors or uncertainty scores describes one particular mix of groups. We study two fixed scores for a common binary target under mixtures of fixed group-conditional laws. Using the cross-group AUC decomposition, we prove that every rational symmetric quadratic comparison geometry is realizable by finite scalar-score distributions. Universal dominance is thus coNP-hard, and even exhaustive checks of every mixture on fewer than $K$ groups can miss a $K$-group reversal. A grid bound gives a dimension-uniform approximation certificate with sharp $1/m$ order. Common score marginals across groups make the comparison numerator linear, with an error envelope for imperfect alignment. These results yield exact finite-bank audits, explicit reversal mixtures and distances, and simultaneous population statements. For failure detection with a frozen ResNet-50 on ImageNet-C, 15 of 18 confidence-score comparisons win in every corruption family on a discovery split, and all 15 are finite-bank certified over all family mixtures on a held-out split; over all 15 corruption types, of 14 discovery winners the corrected grid certifies 10, leaves 3 unresolved, and finds one confirmation reversal of at least 0.05 AUROC. An audit of all 11,019 released Stable LM 2 12B outputs and 35 uncertainty methods finds 66 confirmation-set comparisons that win within all four tasks yet reverse under mixing. Discovery-fitted marginal rank alignment removes all 66; an alignment-error envelope certifies 83 comparisons. Label checks also change several selected reversals. The findings distinguish robustness of frozen scores from robustness after calibration; they do not establish human-error detection, robustness to unseen corruptions, or generalization beyond the evaluated banks.

title: SWE-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Coding
summary: In this work, we study on-policy distillation (OPD) for transferring agentic coding capabilities from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. Prior work has focused primarily on reasoning and short-horizon agentic tasks. We present SWE-OPD, a minimal OPD study for software engineering, where the student interacts with executable repositories and the teacher supervises the prefixes visited by the student. Across three teacher--student pairs, two training sources, and three SWE benchmarks, we find that on-policy supervision transfers coding capability: supervision from Qwen3.6-27B increases the SWE-bench Pro resolve rate of Qwen3.5-9B from 35.9% to 39.4%. Refreshing trajectories is not strictly required either, as an offline variant with cached teacher scores still improves over the student baselines while cutting end-to-end GPU-hours by 59.4%--72.6% and halving peak GPU allocation, at benchmark-dependent accuracy. Furthermore, we extend the offline variant to corss-tokenizer scenarios: distilling GLM-4.5-Air from DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 raises its SWE-bench Pro and Multilingual resolve rate from 35.8% to 39.7% and from 41.8% to 46.2%, around 4% and 4.6% improvement, respectively. We also find that a decreasing loss, however, does not necessarily indicate improved agent performance: under top-$K$ reverse-KL loss, one student exhibits severe repetition despite a decreasing loss. We identify a support-mass gradient term as a potential mechanism underlying this failure.

title: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (poster). 32 pages. Code: https://github.com/Ming-321/PISG
summary: Diffusion-based solvers have become a prominent approach to neural combinatorial optimization. At inference time, they assign each decision variable a prediction score. A greedy decoder ranks candidates by these scores and checks hard constraints to ensure feasibility. Top-ranked candidates should be both promising and jointly feasible, making prediction-constraint alignment critical. When this alignment is weak, greedy decoding skips constraint-violating candidates and falls back to lower-ranked alternatives, degrading solution quality. Existing test-time methods improve search, sampling, or decoding, but do not directly strengthen this alignment before decoding. We observe that trained denoisers already carry constraint-aligned structural signals. Building on this observation, we propose Perturbed Instance-Structure Guidance (PISG), a training-free method that amplifies these signals at test time. At each denoising step, PISG constructs a structure-degraded prediction and extrapolates the unperturbed prediction away from it. The resulting guided prediction improves candidate rankings before constrained decoding. Signal analysis shows that this guidance concentrates on constraint-critical variables rather than uniformly rescaling scores. Under greedy decoding and without downstream refinement, PISG improves all 16 TSP solver-scale pairs across DIFUSCO, T2T, FastT2T, and StruDiCO, and all four MIS-ER solvers, with MIS-ER solved-cost gains up to +4.8%. The gains persist on most large-scale settings after 2-opt, and a preliminary study extends PISG to a Transformer-based solver. These results identify prediction-constraint alignment as an effective test-time enhancement direction for diffusion-based combinatorial optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/Ming-321/PISG.

title: System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs). Cloud LLMs expose patient data. Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come from the request and the schema, then a one-pass decision model answers them. On 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent chose the right tool, or correctly declined, for 97.0% of requests, significantly ahead of all 18 local LLM-agent settings (best 95.2%). The System 1 agent filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values. No System 1 call contained invented content, against 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls. The System 1 Agents framework is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents.

title: Exact Sparse Assignment with Costly Target Embeddings: Fixed-Realization Certificates and an Empirical Audit
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Embedding-based one-to-one association is common in vision and data integration: detections are associated with tracks and records are linked across databases. Such pipelines often solve a sparse optional assignment whose edge scores add a cheap term to an inner product of neural embeddings. When target embeddings are costly, one can acquire them selectively and stop once a certificate proves that the current assignment is optimal. We give such a certificate for unit-norm embeddings. It bounds the unknown part of every reassignment by a support function and maximizes the resulting robust gains with a second sparse assignment; a shared owner-centred bound dominates any fixed-centre triangle bound. We make precise what is certified when network features are not batch-invariant: the realized values of the acquired rows and every unit-ball completion of the rest, not a second forward pass in a different batch. Auditing against a separately batched cache tests a different property; on our first pilot it produced a spurious $2.49\times10^{-6}$ objective failure. We audit the corrected protocol on four public text entity-matching benchmarks with two frozen encoders; no image data is used. All 96 certificate simulations and 120 online selective timings were exact on their own realization (largest objective gap $6.82\times10^{-13}$). At group size 8 the shared certificate acquires on average 60% of candidate-active targets, against 74% (mean centre), 69% (MEB) and 60% (zero centre): it beats the mean and MEB centres but not the zero centre, and savings concentrate in one benchmark (7% acquired). The prespecified runtime claim is contradicted: selective execution is +0.510 s slower per run (dataset-cluster 95% interval [+0.248, +0.772]). Uniform-microbatch re-encodings preserved the optimum in only 5 of 8 encoder-dataset cells, and 45 of 120 online runs disagreed with an eager cache at near-ties.

title: Sage S2.1 Flash Technical Report
summary: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared backbone, which processes them alongside text and images. To develop the model's agent capabilities, we construct verifiable environments for tool use, search, and coding, as well as specialized workflows involving machine learning experiments and scientific software. Task completion is checked against execution results, changes in environment state, or submitted artifacts. We evaluate Sage S1.5 Flash on 33 benchmarks across seven domains. In the primary comparison against five baselines, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench~2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench~II (54.2). These results show particular strengths in using documentary evidence, producing verifiable workbooks, and carrying out machine learning tasks, alongside competitive performance in desktop and browser workflows that require the model to act on visual feedback.

title: How Should Parallel Langevin Chains Share Noise?
summary: Parallel Langevin sampling usually draws an array of independent Gaussian vectors, one row per chain. The average row drives the ensemble mean, with variance $1/K$ per coordinate for $K$ chains. Yet the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) specifies only each row's distribution. Subtracting the column means and rescaling, as in classical antithetic sampling, makes that variance zero. Each chain keeps its ordinary ULA path law for any finite run. For quadratic targets we derive the joint covariance of linear estimates computed from the ensemble mean, including coefficient estimates, time averages and predictions. The identity separates contributions from initial states and Gaussian draws. The coupling changes the second through one scalar, which is zero whenever the draws sum to zero across chains. For nonquadratic targets we bound the remaining variance. Centering has a price: for a quadratic form in the mean-subtracted Gaussian state, the ensemble average has variance $1/(K-1)$ relative to one chain, compared with $1/K$ under independent draws. On three tempered logistic posteriors, eight centered chains reduced the variance of the posterior-mean estimate, summed over coordinates, by two to three orders of magnitude compared with eight independent chains. They also beat 128 independent chains on variance and on variance times sampling time. Under Metropolis correction the reduction shrank to about three- to eightfold: rejected draws no longer balance accepted ones. The measured variance ratios were consistent with a leading-order prediction from rejection frequency and noise energy.

title: Counting What Matters: Reducing Redundant Object Detections in Overlapping UAV Mapping Imagery for Disaster Response
comment: 9 pages, 6 figure, IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics, SSRR 2026, Incheon, Korea, November 02-04, 2026
summary: UAV mapping flights enable rapid aerial reconnaissance of large-scale incident sites in civil protection. However, the image overlap required for orthophoto generation causes every physical object to be detected multiple times across images, while dynamic objects may be omitted from or duplicated in the resulting orthomosaic. Analysis based on the orthophoto alone is therefore structurally insufficient. We address this by detecting objects on the individual images and merging redundant detections across them. This task lies between multi-object tracking and re-identification, as mapping flights form temporally ordered but sparsely sampled sequences with object reappearances across flight strips. We fine-tune YOLO detectors on a new domain-specific nadir dataset from real civil protection operations, roughly doubling mAP50 over the previous system, and propose re-identification approaches based on 3D positions from sparse reconstruction, DINOv3 appearance embeddings, and their combination via constrained greedy clustering. %On four manually annotated real-world mapping flights, the combined weighted multi-pass approach achieves the best trade-off between association accuracy and count error. On four manually annotated real-world mapping flights, an association-only evaluation using ground-truth detections shows that the combined weighted multi-pass approach provides the best trade-off between association quality and count error. It is integrated into the open-source web application ARGUS and visualized as verifiable, correctable object groups for first responders. https://github.com/RoblabWh/argus

title: Eliciting Research Taste in LLMs through Future Research Direction Choice
comment: Accepted at the LM4Sci Workshop at COLM 2026. 23 pages, 7 figures, 18 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/Lossfunk/research-taste-eval-v1
summary: Research taste is increasingly discussed in the context of AI scientists, yet remains little studied or measured in LLMs. This judgment matters especially in open-ended research, where a direction must be chosen before a verifiable objective is available. We operationalize research taste through one task of the scientific workflow: choosing which future research direction to pursue given a research goal and current results. Rather than predicting downstream scientometric metrics or treating author choices as objectively correct, we evaluate models against human-authored future-work directions and report author alignment, stable divergence, and unstable choice as behavioral measures of research-direction preference. We construct an order-controlled evaluation of 80 pairwise comparisons from 19 ML papers published between December 2025 and February 2026 across four subdomains. Each query presents a research goal, hypotheses tested with key results, and two candidate future directions: one author-recommended direction and one plausible distractor sampled from a similar paper. Across eight LLMs, author alignment ranges from 45.0% to 67.5%, while stable divergence ranges from 15.0% to 36.2%. These divergences largely persist under similarity controls, prompt ablations, and an author-preference framing check, and inter-model agreement suggests that some non-author preferences are shared across models. We characterize what models diverge toward using transition-category labels and selected reasoning examples, finding recurring movement toward scaling/generalization and trade-offs between methodological and infrastructure/data extensions. We view this as an early descriptive evaluation for eliciting research taste profiles in LLMs, and as a step toward understanding and steering their research preferences as they take on more autonomous roles in novel open-ended scientific discovery.

title: Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Aligned Action Spaces for Cross-Game Generalization
summary: Zero-shot cross-game generalization aims to consolidate accessible source-game experts into a single vision-language model (VLM) that controls unseen games from raw pixels without target-game parameter updates. While multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) mitigates offline exposure bias and single-game reinforcement learning (RL) overfitting, scaling it to autoregressive VLMs faces two bottlenecks. First, token-to-action misalignment from subword length bias distorts discrete action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Second, multi-teacher policy conflict arises as source teachers under incompatible dynamics issue contradictory closed-loop corrections, causing negative transfer. We propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), a post-training framework that resolves multi-teacher policy conflict within an aligned semantic action space. CAMOPD first uses complete-action alignment to normalize command completion likelihoods over each game's legal action set, forming a calibrated categorical policy that provides reliable uncertainty margins for selective on-policy retention and visual specialist probes that can be evaluated across source games. To resolve policy conflict without target-game data, conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation cross-evaluates these specialists across source games to capture both visual identifiability and inter-teacher compatibility, upweighting compatible teachers while suppressing conflicting corrections. On GameWorld's temporal and directional transfer suites with Qwen3.5-4B, CAMOPD achieves 26/30 (86.7%) and 24/30 (80.0%) Task-1 zero-shot success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, outperforming prompting, weight-merging, and multi-task baselines.

title: The Sense Paradigm for World Models
summary: Latent world models predict the future in an embedding space rather than in pixels. An encoder trained only to predict collapses and maps every observation to the same point, so existing models add a mechanism against collapse, such as a target network, a variance penalty or a distribution penalty. These mechanisms keep the embedding from collapsing, but they leave its distances without meaning, and the model cannot tell a reversible transition from an irreversible one. We propose Sense, a single cross-entropy loss over the directed distance $d(x\to y)=\sum_i \mathrm{ReLU}(y_i-x_i)$ that replaces these mechanisms. The loss avoids collapse on its own, and since the encoder no longer needs the predictor, the predictor is fitted afterwards to fixed embeddings by plain regression. On four pixel environments, the return distance learned by Sense detects irreversible transitions with an AUC between 0.95 and 1.00, where LeWorldModel stays between 0.39 and 0.59. On TwoRoom, the navigation benchmark of LeWorldModel, planning with Sense reaches the goal in 100% of episodes against 91% for LeWorldModel. As the goal moves farther away, the planning failure rate of every baseline grows, while that of Sense stays near zero in Cup, Cliff and Sokoban and is the lowest of all methods in Pendulum.

title: Inference Equivalence and Quotient Coding
